name: Olga Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good afternoon, Olga. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government, and what you tell me is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate the dragline at the open-cut coal mine, which is a walking crane about as tall as a twenty-storey building, with a bucket that lifts a hundred tonnes of dirt. I'm the senior operator, so I train the new ones and I get the tricky digs. Eighteen years on it now. I like the quiet in the cab and the feeling of swinging that bucket exactly where I want it. What wears me out is the twelve-hour nights and the wage freeze we've had for three years.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Karim runs a little tyre and repair shop on the main street, which mostly lives off the mine traffic. Two kids, seven and thirteen, and a mortgage on a brick house with a garden I never have time for. We don't have savings to speak of, maybe enough for one surprise, and the only other big employer is the power station, which isn't hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, that's that then, back to work. I don't really talk about this stuff, and I'm not online except to look at the weather. At work I'd tell the young ones to stop reading the scary articles on their breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, good. I don't use any of those AI things and I don't want to start. If it stays a tool for the office people, the dragline stays mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, which is how I like it. I'd keep training the new operators and keep asking about the wage freeze through the proper channels. Maybe finally fix the garden fence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the dragline stays yours. Has anything already been automated on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They put in a system a few years back that helps with the swing, it does part of the movement on its own. I switch it off when I can, because it's slower than me on the hard digs. The supervisor lets it go because my numbers are good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the worry that's left, if any?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coal itself, really. Everyone knows the mine has a date on it, maybe fifteen years. But that's a different story from robots, that's just the way things are going.

S0.say: I'd say that's settled and get back to work, without much talk. At work I'd tell the young operators to stop reading scary articles on their breaks.
S0.think: Privately I'd be glad, because I don't use AI and don't want to. If it stays an office tool, the dragline stays mine.
S0.do: Keeps working and training new operators exactly as before, raising the wage freeze through the usual channels. Perhaps fixes the garden fence.
S0.quote: I switch it off when I can, because it's slower than me on the hard digs.
S0.fieldNote: Olga prefers no change and already resists the swing-assist system on her own machine. She separates AI from the slower, expected end of coal, which she accepts as normal. She is pragmatic and not at all political in tone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see how it goes, there's no point panicking until we know what they're bringing in. If someone asked at the pub I'd say the dragline is the last thing they'll manage to automate. That's what I'd want to believe, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think they'd turn on that swing system full-time and make one operator run the dragline from an office, maybe two machines at once. And I'm the one who switches it off, so I'm not exactly first in line for that office job. That's the bit that bothers me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back straight away, the cable TV and the second car insurance, and try to put away a few hundred over the year. I'd keep doing my job as well as I can, because good numbers kept me safe so far. If they made the training compulsory, I'd go, but I wouldn't volunteer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, quietly. Like a noise in the engine you can't find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't volunteer for the training. Why not, if it might keep you in a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm forty-three and I'm very good at one thing. Learning screens at my age, I'd be slow and I'd look stupid in front of the people I trained. Maybe that's wrong, but it's how I feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean for Karim's shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer workers driving in means fewer tyres and fewer oil changes, simple as that. He's already worried about electric cars needing less work. So it's two hits on one kitchen table.

S1.say: I'd say there's no point panicking until we know what they're bringing in. At the pub I'd claim the dragline is the last machine they'll manage to automate.
S1.think: I really think they'd run the swing system full-time and have one operator run the dragline from an office. As the one who switches it off, I'm not first in line for that office job.
S1.do: Cuts the cable TV and second car insurance to save a few hundred over the year. Keeps her output high and would attend compulsory training but not volunteer for it.
S1.feel: Quietly anxious, like an engine noise she can't locate.
S1.quote: So it's two hits on one kitchen table.
S1.fieldNote: Olga's public calm hides a clear private read: her refusal of the assist system could cost her the remote seat. She won't volunteer for training out of fear of looking slow in front of people she trained. Her husband's shop doubles the household's exposure to fewer mine workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd say. Probably that someone in charge should have seen it coming, the government, the company, all of them. I'm not one for marches, but I'd want somebody to explain what the plan is for towns like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's over. Two years, the mine runs itself, the shop loses its customers, and we've got nothing in the bank. I can't see what I'd do, and that's the honest answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the bank and the mine's payroll office in the first week to find out what redundancy I'd get, because that's the only money we'd have. I'd sell my car and Karim would keep the shop open as long as he could. I'd probably ring my sister about moving in with her, though she's in a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. Like the ground just isn't there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a typical evening look like at home, in that first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karim and I doing sums at the kitchen table after the kids are asleep. The thirteen-year-old would know something was wrong, she always does. I'd stop sleeping, I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you would try that you wouldn't normally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd do the training after all, if there was any training. But in two years there wouldn't even be anything to train for. That's what makes it so bad, there's no door to walk through.

S2.say: I'd say somebody in charge, government or company, should have seen this coming. I'm not one for marches, but I'd want someone to explain the plan for towns like ours.
S2.think: I honestly think it's over for us in two years: the mine runs itself, the shop loses customers and we have no savings. I can't see what I'd do.
S2.do: Goes to the bank and payroll office in the first week to learn her redundancy terms. Sells her car while Karim keeps the shop open as long as possible, and asks her sister about moving in.
S2.feel: Panicked, as if the ground has disappeared, and unable to sleep.
S2.quote: In two years there wouldn't even be anything to train for. That's what makes it so bad, there's no door to walk through.
S2.fieldNote: With two years, Olga has no plan and says so plainly. Her only levers are redundancy money, selling the car and family. Interestingly, the speed made her willing to train for the first time, but she saw nothing to train for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so the company and the council need to sit down with us and make a real plan. I'd go to a meeting if there was one, which is more than I usually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have maybe three years left on the dragline, if I'm lucky and if I stop switching off the system. That's three years to save something. But after that I don't know what a forty-eight-year-old dragline operator does in this town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the swing system properly, even though I hate it, so I'm not the first one out. We'd save every spare bit, maybe a hundred and fifty a month, which is a lot for us. And Karim and I would talk about whether the shop could do something else, like servicing the mine's robot vehicles, if they'd let him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but it's a slower alarm. Like a warning siren you can hear from far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd start using the system you hate. What changes your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fear, mostly. With two years there's no point; with five years, being the operator who fights the machine is a good way to get picked off first. I'd swallow my pride for three years of wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about their own futures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To not count on the mine, like I did and my father did. The thirteen-year-old likes animals, maybe a vet nurse. I wouldn't know what to tell the seven-year-old yet.

S3.say: I'd say there are a few years, so the company and the council need to sit down with workers and make a real plan. I'd go to a meeting, which is more than I usually do.
S3.think: I think I'd have maybe three years left on the dragline if I stop switching off the assist system. After that, I don't know what a forty-eight-year-old dragline operator does in this town.
S3.do: Starts using the swing-assist system properly to avoid being first out. Saves about a hundred and fifty a month and talks with Karim about the shop servicing the mine's robot vehicles.
S3.feel: Alarmed, but in a slower way, like a siren heard from far off.
S3.quote: I'd swallow my pride for three years of wages.
S3.fieldNote: Five years makes Olga do something she refused in milder pictures: use the automation on her own machine. Her reason is fear of being picked off first, not new enthusiasm. She is starting to steer her children away from the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and coal might be gone by then anyway. I'd tell people to keep their heads and plan, not panic. That's the sensible line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's still bad for me, just slower. In ten years I'm fifty-three, and I'd have spent a decade dreading it. But the kids would be older and the mortgage smaller, so it's not the cliff the two-year one is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and use the system so I last. Maybe in year three or four I'd do a course, something practical like forklift and warehouse, because I can't see myself in an office. And we'd try to pay a bit extra off the mortgage every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, but it would sit in the back of my head for ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe in year three or four. Why not straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm still earning on the dragline and I'd rather not until I have to. I know that's what everyone says and then it's too late. I'm being honest, that's what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to hear from, in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company, straight, with dates. Not the politicians, they say whatever gets them through the next vote. If the mine manager stood up and said, this is the plan, here's the year your machine goes, I'd believe that.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time and coal might be gone by then anyway. I'd tell people to keep their heads and plan rather than panic.
S4.think: I think it's still bad for me, only slower, and I'd be fifty-three after a decade of dread. With older kids and a smaller mortgage, though, it isn't the cliff of the two-year picture.
S4.do: Keeps doing the job and uses the assist system so she lasts. Plans a practical course such as forklift and warehouse work in year three or four, and pays a little extra off the mortgage each year.
S4.feel: Anxious in the back of her mind, without panic.
S4.quote: If the mine manager stood up and said, this is the plan, here's the year your machine goes, I'd believe that.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years eases Olga to steady anxiety, but she admits she would still delay retraining until forced, knowing that's a common mistake. She trusts plain information from the company far more than politicians. Her realistic fallback is warehouse work, not an office.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There'd be nothing to plan and nowhere to go. What would help is a straight answer early, from the company, about when and how, and a decent redundancy payment so we're not losing the house while we work out what's next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what we'd lose that isn't money. The dragline crew is like family, we've covered for each other through funerals and births. A machine doesn't do that, and nobody's going to pay to replace it.

headlineQuote: A machine doesn't do that, and nobody's going to pay to replace it.
portrait: Olga Haddad is a 43-year-old senior dragline operator at an open-cut coal mine, married to a man whose tyre shop depends on mine traffic, with two children, a mortgage and almost no savings. She avoids new technology, even switching off the swing-assist on her own machine, and stays calm only if AI goes nowhere. Under steady change she becomes quietly anxious and would wait until training was compulsory, and the two-year AGI picture leaves her panicked with no door to walk through. Given five or ten years she reluctantly accepts the automation to keep her wages, plans late and practically, and wants straight dates from the company rather than promises from politicians.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there would be nothing to plan and nowhere to go.
whatWouldHelp: An early, straight answer from the company about when and how automation comes, and a decent redundancy payment so they don't lose the house.
